summary: This experimental document specifies a multicast handover optimization for Proxy Mobile IPv6 called SIAL. It speeds up delivery of multicast traffic to mobile nodes after they move, by acquiring subscription information through the Local Mobility Anchor.

eli5.summary: When you move seats, your show should keep playing. This helps the network learn what you were watching faster so it resumes quickly.

questions: mld query delay in mobile networks
subtitle: Speed up multicast delivery during mobile handovers using subscription information from the network.

tldr.problem: When a mobile node moves between access gateways in a PMIPv6 network while receiving multicast, it experiences a gap in service while the new gateway learns what multicast groups the node subscribes to.
tldr.mechanism: SIAL (Subscription Information Acquisition through the LMA) extends PMIPv6 signaling to carry multicast subscription information directly between gateways through the Local Mobility Anchor, avoiding delays from standard MLD query-response cycles.
tldr.outcome: Mobile nodes can resume receiving multicast content quickly after handover, with support for both proactive and reactive handovers. The solution is Experimental and works with existing PMIPv6 deployments.

today: RFC 7161 is an Experimental specification published in March 2014. It provides handover optimization for multicast in PMIPv6 domains and has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: The Multicast Handover Problem
sections.content:
Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) is a network-based mobility management protocol that allows mobile nodes to move between access points without managing their own routing. When a mobile node is receiving multicast content and moves to a new access gateway, it experiences a delay before the new gateway learns what multicast groups the node is subscribed to and starts delivering that content again.

The base solution for multicast in PMIPv6 (RFC 6224) relies on the standard Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) protocol. When a mobile node attaches to a new gateway, the gateway sends an MLD General Query to discover the node's active subscriptions. The node responds with an MLD Report, but this exchange can take several seconds (up to 10 seconds by default), during which the mobile node receives no multicast data. This delay is caused by the time to detect attachment, re-establish the data plane, radio transfer delays, and the MLD query response interval.

SIAL (Subscription Information Acquisition through the LMA) solves this by having the network itself maintain and quickly share the mobile node's multicast subscription information during handover, independent of the mobile node's response time.
sections.eli5: The old way made the new gateway ask the phone what shows it wanted. The phone might not answer fast. The new way has the network remember, so there is no waiting.

sections.title: How SIAL Works
sections.content:
The key insight of SIAL is that the Local Mobility Anchor (LMA)—the central mobility manager—is in the best position to keep track of each mobile node's multicast subscriptions. During a handover, the LMA already knows which gateway the node is leaving and which one it is joining. It can quickly acquire the node's current multicast context from the old gateway and immediately pass it to the new gateway.

SIAL works in two scenarios: proactive handovers, where the old gateway notifies the LMA of the node's departure before the node attaches to the new gateway, and reactive handovers, where the new gateway registers the node before the LMA hears from the old one. In proactive handovers, the old gateway includes the multicast subscription information when it sends the de-registration message. The LMA stores this information and sends it back when the new gateway registers the node. In reactive handovers, the LMA sends a query message to the old gateway asking for the node's subscriptions, and the old gateway responds with that information.

The solution only updates the multicast context during handovers, not continuously while the node is attached. This minimizes signaling overhead while ensuring the information is current at the critical moment.
sections.eli5: The LMA remembers what shows each phone was watching. When a phone moves, the LMA tells the new gateway right away what to send.

sections.title: Protocol Extensions: Options and Messages
sections.content:
SIAL adds three main extensions to PMIPv6:

1. Active Multicast Subscription Option: A new TLV-encoded option that carries multicast subscription information. It uses the format from MLD or IGMP reports, so one option represents one multicast group subscription. The option includes a field indicating whether it is MLDv1 or MLDv2 format.

2. Multicast Signaling Flag (S flag): A new flag in the Proxy Binding Update (PBU) and Proxy Binding Acknowledgement (PBA) messages. The S flag indicates whether the gateway supports multicast signaling. If S=1, the gateway can handle multicast subscription information. If S=0, it does not. This flag enables backward compatibility with gateways that do not support SIAL.

3. Subscription Query and Response Messages: Two new mobility header messages (values 22 and 23) for exchanging multicast subscription information when needed. The LMA sends a Subscription Query to ask for a node's multicast context; the previous gateway responds with a Subscription Response message containing all active subscriptions. These messages are used primarily in reactive handover scenarios.

The PBA message in the LMA may also include a new timer (PBA timer) that limits how long the LMA waits to gather multicast information before sending the acknowledgement to the new gateway, preventing multicast delays from blocking unicast delivery.
sections.eli5: The network adds three things: a label for subscription info, a flag to say if a gateway can handle subscriptions, and two messages to ask and answer 'what is this phone watching?'

sections.title: Proactive and Reactive Handovers
sections.content:
Proactive Handover (when the old gateway knows the node is leaving first): The old gateway sends a de-registration message with the S flag set to 1 and includes one Active Multicast Subscription option for each group the node is subscribed to. The LMA receives and stores this information. When the new gateway later sends its registration message (with S=1), the LMA immediately includes all the stored subscription information in its acknowledgement. The new gateway then joins the multicast groups on behalf of the node. No extra query is needed.

Reactive Handover (when the new gateway registers the node first): The new gateway sends its registration message with S=1, but it does not know the node's multicast subscriptions yet. Before acknowledging, the LMA sends a Subscription Query message to the old gateway asking what groups the node is subscribed to. The old gateway responds with a Subscription Response message listing all active subscriptions using Active Multicast Subscription options. The LMA then sends the new gateway an acknowledgement that includes all this information. If the old gateway has already forgotten the node's subscriptions (because the node detached before the LMA's query arrived), the response indicates I=0 (no information available), and the new gateway falls back to the standard MLD query method.

To prevent multicast acquisition delays from blocking unicast traffic, the LMA SHOULD implement the PBA timer mechanism. This timer limits how long the LMA waits for multicast information before sending the unicast acknowledgement to the new gateway, allowing unicast traffic to flow immediately while multicast subscription information can arrive separately.
sections.eli5: Two paths: the old gateway can say goodbye with the subscription list, or the new gateway can ask for it. Either way, multicast resumes much faster than waiting for the phone to respond.

sections.title: IPv4 Support and Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
SIAL supports both IPv6 and IPv4 multicast. For IPv4, mobile nodes use the Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) instead of MLD, and the network-side components use IGMP proxy functions in place of MLD proxy. The subscription information is structured the same way; the Active Multicast Subscription option simply carries IGMP group addresses instead of IPv6 multicast group addresses.

The solution is designed to coexist with existing PMIPv6 multicast deployments and other optimization schemes. It does not replace the standard MLD/IGMP discovery mechanism but complements it, allowing legacy nodes and gateways to continue working while new implementations can benefit from faster handovers. Gateways that do not support SIAL (indicated by S=0 in their messages) continue to use the original MLD query method. The solution also works alongside other PMIPv6 multicast optimizations such as route optimization schemes (RFC 7028).
sections.eli5: It works the same for IPv4 and IPv6. Old phones and gateways that don't know about this still work fine.
